# Workflow

Workflow is a system to make it easier on your brain to do your work. Don't waste time finding things or trying to remember that great idea you had.

. . .

::: {.big}
A **keystone habit**: the one habit that organizes all the other good habits
:::

# Project notebooks

Organize your projects into notebooks or folders of some kind. Notion, OneNote, text files in a folder, or a paper journal all work.


# Project notebooks: my system

Three folders under `research-projects/`, and a project moves through them in order.

::::: {.flow}
:::: {.step}
💡

**Pending**

`_future-ideas/`, one folder per idea. A conversation with Claude first, then a note to Google Drive
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
🔬

**Ongoing**

`research-projects/`, one folder per project, the skeleton on the next slide
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
✅

**Completed**

`_completed/` once the paper is accepted, `_stalled/` if it never gets there
::::
:::::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room before revealing the flow: where do your half-formed ideas live right now? Phone notes, a notebook, nowhere?
:::


# Project folders

Key is to have a system where files are named appropriately and everything is easily accessible. Basically it's a closet for your research.


# Project folders

Every one of my projects starts from the same skeleton. One command builds it, so no two projects are organized differently.

::: {.tree}
```
📁 project
├── 📄 README.md
├── 📁 paper/            paper.tex or paper.qmd, plus the bibliography
├── 📁 presentations/
├── 📁 data/
│   ├── 📁 input/        raw, never modified by code
│   └── 📁 output/       cleaned, analysis-ready
├── 📁 code/
│   ├── 📁 data-build/   input → output
│   └── 📁 analysis/     output → results
├── 📁 results/
│   ├── 📁 tables/
│   └── 📁 figures/
├── 📁 background/       literature, PDFs
├── 📁 notes/            planning, decisions
└── 📁 scratch/          throwaway
```
:::

::: {.popup .fragment}
**`data/input/` is all symbolic links**

- Raw data lives once, in `research-data/`, one folder per dataset
- Cleaned panels live in data-only repos, `research-data-repo/`
- A project `ln -s`'s what it needs. No copies, nothing modified
:::


# Project folders

- Project need not start out perfectly organized
- Think of the folder/file structure as your kitchen
    - It will get dirty
    - Don't let it get so dirty that you forget stuff
    - Clean up regularly!

# Why bother?

This part is all about transparency and reproducibility (for your future self and for others). Some other resources...

- [Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences](https://www.bitss.org/)
- [Julian Reif's Guide for Replication with Stata](https://reifjulian.github.io/guide/)


# Reproducibility

- You'll need to come back to this one day!
- Others will (hopefully) ask you about this

. . .

::: {.big}
"I lost my hard drive" is unacceptable
:::


# Automation

One benefit of good tracking and workflow is that you partially automate your projects...

- No repeating commands in the command line
- No copying and pasting values into tables
- No copying and pasting values into the text (harder to do)


. . .

My version: one driver script per pipeline (`_build-all.R`, `_analyze-all.R`) that sources the numbered steps in order. One command reruns everything.


# Naming files {.center}

Avoid spaces in file names. Avoid them at all costs. *DO NOT PUT SPACES IN YOUR FILE NAMES.*

. . .

::: {.big}
"A space in a file name is a space in your soul."
:::


# Naming files

Avoid things like this...

::: {.tree}
```
📁 great-research-idea
├── 📁 analysis
│   ├── 📄 final_analysis.R
│   ├── 📄 final_final_analysis.R     ❌
│   └── 📄 last_analysis.R            ❌
├── 📁 data
│   ├── 📄 clean_data.csv
│   └── 📄 extra_clean_data.csv       ❌
└── 📁 paper
    ├── 📄 draft1.tex
    ├── 📄 final_draft.tex
    └── 📄 final_final_draft.tex      ❌
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Show of hands: who has a file called final_final or v7 somewhere right now?
:::


# Naming files

- Use dates in your filenames if necessary (YYYYMMDD format)
- Minimize the use of filename dates and instead try official version control
- Dates useful in log files and similar output (not under version control)


. . .

Related point...use common sense (but short) variable names without spaces


# Data workflow

Some quick thoughts on workflow...

::: {.steps .incremental}
1. Avoid absolute path names.
2. If you use the same data across projects, link to it (`ln -s`) rather than copying it
3. Separate your analysis and your markdown (not practical otherwise)
4. **NEVER** delete or directly change raw data files
:::

# Why bother with version control?


1. Internal validity (replicability for your future self)
2. External validity (replicability for others)


. . .

**note**: particularly important on the modern job market


# Version control

How do you track your versions? Don't keep two versions of the same thing.

::::: {.flow}
:::: {.step}
📂

**Dropbox, Google Drive**

Some form of version history, but incomplete
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
✍️

**Overleaf**

Built-in version history, for the paper only
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
🐙

**Git / GitHub**

Every file, every change, and shareable, so you get external validity too
::::
:::::


# Virtual environments

Let's assume your code works on your system. You (should) also want it to work on other computers. How do you get other computers to look like your own?

. . .

:::: {.cards .three}
::: {.card}
**🐳 Docker**

Basically mimic your entire machine
:::
::: {.card}
**📦 renv**

Record the version of every R package in a `.lock` file
:::
::: {.card}
**🐍 renv + Python**

`renv::use_python()` does the same for a virtual Python environment
:::
::::

# Writing the paper

Same folders either way. The only difference is the paper file and who else can write to it.

:::: {.cards .two}
::: {.card}
**✍️ Solo**

- `paper/paper.qmd`
- Tables, figures, and numbers come in from `results/`
- One render builds the PDF
:::
::: {.card}
**👥 Co-authored**

- `paper/paper.tex`, synced with Overleaf through GitHub
- Overleaf syncs `paper/` and `presentations/` only (next slide)
:::
::::


# Which folders Overleaf can change

::: {.tree}
```
📁 project
├── 📄 .gitignore        ← the first filter
├── 📁 paper/             ✅ tracked, Overleaf syncs here
├── 📁 presentations/     ✅ tracked, Overleaf syncs here
├── 📁 code/              🚫 tracked, but guarded — Overleaf can't touch it
├── 📁 results/           🚫 tracked, but guarded
├── 📁 data/              ⛔ gitignored — never even reaches GitHub
├── 📁 notes/             ⛔ gitignored
├── 📁 background/        ⛔ gitignored
└── 📁 scratch/           ⛔ gitignored
```
:::

. . .

Two filters. `.gitignore` keeps data, notes, background, and scratch off GitHub, so Overleaf never sees them. A GitHub Action then blocks any Overleaf commit that touches `code/` or `results/`.


# Using AI {.smaller}

Most of my code and a lot of my notes now start as a conversation with Claude.

:::: {.cards .three}
::: {.card}
**🤖 What it does**

- Writes the code from my instructions (lots of safeguards and checks here)
- Builds the project skeleton and the driver scripts
- Summarizes papers and drafts the notes
:::
::: {.card}
**🔍 What I check**

- Every number in the paper (tracked in a ledger)
- Every citation is a paper I've reviewed
- Many checks (some automated) on data cleanup/management steps and common analysis
:::
::: {.card}
**✍️ What I do**

- Form the research question and the identification
- Interpreting results along the way, updating analyses as needed
- The writing. Journals ask now, and all AI tools still write poorly
:::
::::

. . .

AI can still make things up when it doesn't know the answer. It's better at citing real papers, but it can still miss the point of those papers or get the interpretation of a result/analysis way way off. Check its work the way you'd check a new RA's.

# If your laptop died tonight, what would you lose? {.center}

. . .

Three ways to make the answer "nothing."

::: {.notes}
Show of hands before moving on: who has a backup that would actually survive this? Then: when did it last run?
:::


# Three options {.smaller}

:::: {.cards .three}
::: {.card}
**💽 External hard drive**

- ✅ Affordable and fully in your control
- ✅ Data remain private
- ❌ Only backed up when you remember
- ❌ Can be slow
- ❌ Same physical place as the laptop
:::
::: {.card}
**☁️ Cloud service**

Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive

- ✅ Works painlessly in the background
- ✅ Easy to share when needed
- ✅ Emory's OneDrive: free, 5 TB, and certified for sensitive data (HIPAA)
- ❌ Personal accounts get expensive, and can't hold restricted data
:::
::: {.card}
**🗄️ Your own NAS**

Just build your own network!

- ✅ Data stay with you, backed up in real time
- ✅ Redundancy built in
- ❌ Expensive to buy
- ❌ Harder to set up
:::
::::

. . .

Crashes will inevitably happen between backups.
